phonemes.desc: aspirated pʰ — a 'p' released with breath, not an English 'f' — plus the diphthong oi as in οἶκος; the acute accent means the voice rises across this syllable
voiced b followed by long eta (η), an open 'eh' held twice the length of a short vowel — never the English 'ee' the modern name has drifted to

pronunciation.approximation: 'FOY-beh' — the first syllable rhymes with 'boy' and carries the rising pitch; the second is a long, open 'eh', not 'bee'.

kin.label: Greek
kin.form: φοῖβος (phoîbos), 'bright, shining, pure' — the masculine form, Apollo's standing epithet, which Aeschylus derives outright from her name (Eumenides 7–8)

kin.label: PIE
kin.form: *bʰeh₂- 'to shine, appear' (compare φαίνω, 'to bring to light', φάος, 'light') — proposed but contested; Beekes and Chantraine both treat the derivation cautiously

pronunciation.note: Tier-1: the Greek Φοίβη carries both an accent (the acute on the diphthong οί) and a long vowel (η), so the restoration Phoíbē preserves stress and quantity together — two facts of the name that plain ASCII 'Phoebe' silently erases.

domains.title: The Third Voice of Delphi
domains.subtitle: Titaness of Prophecy, Keeper of the Oracle before Apollo
domains.lead: Phoíbē is the Titaness of prophecy, the 'shining one' whose name is simply the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright'. Before Apollo ever spoke at Delphi, the Pythia's own prayer names her the oracle's third keeper — after Gaia and Themis — who passed the seat to her grandson as a birthday gift. She is light as foresight: the radiance that sees before it shines.

cards.name: The Oracular Seat
cards.desc: Aeschylus gives Delphi's succession as Earth, then Themis, then Phoíbē — who yields the seat to Apollo as a birthday gift (Eumenides 1–8).

cards.name: Prophetic Light
cards.desc: Her name is the feminine of Phoîbos, 'the bright one' — the shining, prophetic power she hands down to her grandson.

cards.name: The Golden Line
cards.desc: Daughter of Ouranos and Gaia, wife of Koios, mother of Lētō — grandmother of Apollo and Ártemis (Theogony 404–410).

symbols.name: Golden Crown
symbols.meaning: Hesiod's sole epithet for her in the Titan catalogue — Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον, 'Phoebe of the golden crown' (Theogony 136): the royalty of the eldest generation, and light worn on the brow.

symbols.name: Delphic Tripod
symbols.meaning: The Pythia's three-legged seat at Delphi, which Aeschylus' succession makes hers third, after Gaia and Themis (Eumenides 1–8) — the one concrete object to which her mythic tenure attaches.

symbols.name: Omphalos
symbols.meaning: The navel-stone marking Delphi as the center of the world; part of the sanctuary landscape of the oracle she held and handed on. She has no independent iconography — her attributes are Delphi's.

symbols.name: Laurel
symbols.meaning: The prophetic tree of Delphi, inherited by Apollo together with the seat she gave him; with her it marks the continuity of the shrine rather than a personal emblem.

symbols.name: Prophetic Radiance
symbols.meaning: Her name itself — the feminine of φοῖβος, 'bright, shining' — is her symbol: light understood as foresight, the gleam that sees ahead.

symbols.name: The Moon
symbols.meaning: A late association: Roman poets use Phoebē as a name of the moon paired with Phoebus the sun, and through her granddaughter Artemis she drifts lunar. Ancient, but poetic rather than cultic.

mythology.lead: Phoíbē stands quietly at the hinge of Greek myth: a Titan of the eldest generation whose role is to inherit and to hand on — the oracle to Apollo, the bloodline to Lētō. Her myths are genealogies that glow: everything she touches passes light forward.

myths.title: Golden-Crowned among the Titans
myths.text: In the Theogony (132–136), Hesiod catalogues the twelve Titans born to Ouranos and Gaia — Ocean, Koios, Krios, Hyperion, Iapetus, Theia, Rheia, Themis, Mnemosyne, Tethys, and Kronos — and among them 'Phoíbē of the golden crown' (Φοίβην τε χρυσοστέφανον). She is one of the few in the list to carry an epithet at all, and the epithet is made of light. Hesiod records no deed of hers: the eldest Titans are not actors but origins, the generation from which the Olympian world descends. Yet the golden crown deserves its weight. Where her brothers' names speak of violence waiting to happen, her crown is royal without a battle — the one piece of regalia in the catalogue that no one contests. Later tradition made the point explicit: Aeschylus will have her hold Delphi 'with her consent, and by no violence,' and the serenity of Hesiod's epithet seems to know it already. She is sovereignty as inheritance, not conquest.

myths.title: The Much-Desired Couch of Koios
myths.text: Later in the Theogony (404–410), 'Phoíbē ascended the much-desired couch of Koios' (Φοίβη δ' αὖ Κοίου πολυήρατον ἷξε λέχος εἰσαναβᾶσα) and conceived Lētō — 'dark-robed, gentle, the mildest of all who dwell on Olympus.' The line continues without pause: Lētō bears 'Apollo and arrow-pouring Artemis' to Zeus (Theogony 918–920), so Phoíbē stands at the head of the Delphic family, grandmother to the two Olympians of light. Notice the pattern Hesiod never states: a bright Titaness marries an inquisitive one — Koios, whose very name means 'query, intelligence' — and from their union comes Lētō, the mother the whole tradition calls 'gentle.' Intelligence wed to radiance produces gentleness, and gentleness produces the gods of prophecy and the hunt. Hesiod gives the marriage no quarrel and no story beyond the bed and the child; for a Titaness of the first generation, the genealogy is the myth.

myths.title: The Third Voice of Delphi
myths.text: The opening lines of Aeschylus' Eumenides (1–8) preserve her greatest role. The Pythia, praying at Delphi before she gives her oracle, names Gaia 'first of prophets' and Themis second upon her mother's seat; third — 'with her consent, and by no violence' — sat 'another Titan, a child of Earth, Phoíbē.' Phoíbē then gave the throne to Apollo 'as a birthday gift' (γενέθλιον δόσιν), 'and he bears his name Phoíbos as a namesake from hers' (τὸ Φοίβης δ' ὄνομ' ἔχει παρώνυμον). It is the only peaceful succession in the violent history of the Greek gods. Ouranos falls to Kronos by the sickle; Kronos falls to Zeus by war; even Delphi's own older traditions remember an Apolline takeover stained by the dragon's blood. But in the tragedian's version the oracle changes hands as a family inheritance — grandmother to grandson, by gift, on a birthday — and the new god's most famous epithet is simply his grandmother's name, passed down like a ring. The Greeks seem to have felt that foresight, unlike kingship, could not be seized; it had to be bequeathed.

myths.title: Two Daughters of Prophecy
myths.text: Apollodorus (Library 1.4.1) gives her motherhood its full shape: from Koios and Phoíbē spring two daughters, Asteria and Lētō. Asteria, 'the starry one,' bears Hekátē to Perses (Theogony 409–412), the torch-bearing goddess of crossroads whom Zeus honors above all the gods; Lētō bears Apollo and Artemis. Through one daughter flows the lineage of night sky and moonlight — Hekátē is Phoíbē's granddaughter as truly as Apollo is — through the other the lineage of sunlit prophecy. Both of Delphi's lights, and both of the moon's names, are in effect Phoíbē's grandchildren. The catalogue logic is the point: prophecy, starlight, the crossroads, and the hunt all descend from one bright Titaness, so that the whole nocturnal economy of the younger gods reads as her household's output. Hesiod calls her golden-crowned; her daughters and granddaughters are the crown's jewels.

myths.title: The Starry Sister
myths.text: Phoíbē's other daughter never reached Olympus. Apollodorus (Library 1.4.1) names her Asteria — 'the starry one' — sister of Lētō, beloved of Zeus, who fled his pursuit by throwing herself into the sea in the shape of a quail (ortux); the island that rose where she fell the poets called Ortygia, later Delos (Callimachus, Hymn to Delos 36–40). It was this floating, rootless island — the wandering fragment of the starry sister — that gave Lētō refuge when no fixed land dared receive her, and so became the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis. Thus Phoíbē's two daughters map the whole heaven: Asteria supplies the ground, Lētō the children — one lineage of night sky, one of daylight prophecy — and the shining god of Delphi and the huntress of the moon are, through both lines, her grandchildren. The myth means that even the earth that receives the gods was once a fleeing girl: stability, in this family, is what a pursued sister becomes when she stops running.

lore.syncretism: Phoíbē never received a Roman cult of her own; Rome met her inside Apollo, whose Greek epithet Phoebus became a standard poetic name — and whose name Aeschylus had already declared to be hers (Eumenides 7–8). In Latin poetry the feminine Phoebē then hardens into a name of the moon itself, paired with Phoebus the sun, so the Titaness survives in Rome as a word rather than a worship. Through her granddaughter Artemis–Diana, later poets quietly fold her into the lunar goddess, but the equation remains poetic, never cultic, and no ancient author confuses the two genealogies.
lore.culturalLegacy: The name lives on in English as Phoebe — entering the Christian tradition through Phoíbē of Cenchreae, the deaconess Paul commends to the Roman church (Romans 16:1) — and it has been one of the most durable classical given names in the language ever since. Astronomy keeps the Titaness herself: Phoebe, the dark retrograde outer moon of Saturn discovered by W. H. Pickering in 1899, is named for her, a fitting moon for the Titaness of light. And whenever literature writes 'Phoebus Apollo', it repeats — whether it knows it or not — her name, which Aeschylus says Apollo took from his grandmother. The small American flycatcher called the phoebe, by contrast, is named for its call: a false friend, not a descendant.
lore.extendedMeditation: Phoíbē is nearly invisible in Greek worship, and that invisibility is the point: her significance is structural rather than devotional. She is the lawful transmission of prophecy. In a myth-world built on violent succession — Ouranos castrated by Kronos, Kronos overthrown by Zeus — Aeschylus makes hers the sole peaceful one: the oracle passes 'with consent and by no violence', as a gift, and even leaves its name behind as a family inheritance. The Greeks seem to have felt that foresight, unlike kingship, could not be seized; it had to be bequeathed. Her shining is therefore not the blaze of the sun but the quiet lamp of knowledge kept burning across generations — from Earth, through law in Themis, through her, into Apollo's daylight.

sources.name: Beekes, Robert, and Chantraine, Pierre — s.v. φοῖβος
Pausanias 10.5.5–7 (the older oracle of Earth and Themis)

lore.archaeology: Phoíbē has no temple, sanctuary, or cult image of her own anywhere in the Greek world — she belongs to genealogy and to Delphi's remembered past rather than to ritual. Her setting is the sanctuary of Apollo at Delphi, where French excavations since 1892 have uncovered the Archaic and Classical temples above the adyton in which the Pythia sat, the very seat whose pre-Apolline tenants the Pythia lists in Aeschylus' prologue; Pausanias (10.5.5–7) records the parallel Delphic tradition of an older oracle of Earth and Themis, passed on until Apollo held it. The omphalos copies and tripod dedications in the Delphi museum are the material shadow of the throne she is said to have kept third.
